title: What the first week in a sober living house actually looks like
author: Admin
excerpt: Most people arrive braced for rules and inspections. The first week is quieter than that: sleep, meals at regular times, and learning where the mugs live.
intro: People usually arrive expecting either a boot camp or a hostel. It is neither. The first few days are mostly administrative and surprisingly dull, which is exactly what most arrivals need.
You get a room, a tour, a copy of the house agreement and a first conversation with your key worker. Nobody asks you to tell your story to a room full of strangers on day one.
sectionText: Sleep is usually the first thing to sort itself out, and it takes longer than people expect. Quiet hours exist for that reason, and they are one of the few rules nobody argues with after the first fortnight.

quote.text: I spent my first three days waiting for someone to tell me off. By the end of the week I realised the structure was not aimed at me, it was just how the house worked.
quote.author: Former resident

afterQuote: The other thing that surprises people is how ordinary it feels. Someone is cooking, someone is watching television, someone has gone to bed early. That ordinariness is doing a lot of quiet work.
bullets: ID and any paperwork from treatment or probation
A month of any prescribed medication, in its original packaging
Clothes for work or interviews, not just for the house
Phone numbers written down somewhere other than your phone
closing: By the end of week two most residents have a rhythm: chores on a set day, the house meeting on a set evening, check-ins that stop feeling like a test.
If week one feels strange, that is not a sign it is going badly. Almost everyone describes the same thing.

title: Why curfews help more than they restrict
author: Admin
excerpt: A curfew sounds like something imposed on you. Residents tend to describe it differently once they have lived with one for a month.
intro: Of all the house rules, the curfew is the one people push back on hardest at the start. It sounds like being treated as a child, and nobody arrives wanting that.
What residents usually say later is that the curfew removed a decision rather than a freedom.
sectionText: Relapse rarely begins with a plan. It begins with an unplanned hour late at night, an old contact, and nothing in particular to go home for. A curfew quietly takes that hour off the table.

quote.text: The curfew is the reason I came home on the nights I did not want to. There was no debate to have with myself, because the debate was already settled.
quote.author: Resident

afterQuote: It also means somebody notices. A missed curfew prompts a phone call, and that call has interrupted more than one night that was heading somewhere bad.
bullets: The same time for everyone, staff included in the planning
Adjusted in advance for shift work or family commitments
A missed curfew starts a conversation, not an eviction
Reviewed with your key worker as you progress
closing: Rules that exist to catch people out breed dishonesty. Rules that exist to make the week predictable do the opposite.
Residents who stay long enough almost always end up defending the curfew to newer arrivals, which is a better advert for it than anything we could write.

title: Cooking for yourself again, and why it matters
author: Admin
excerpt: More honest conversations happen over washing up than in any formal session. The kitchen does a lot of quiet work in a recovery house.
intro: Plenty of people arrive having not cooked a proper meal in years. Addiction tends to replace eating with something quicker, and the skill disappears without anyone noticing.
The kitchen is shared, and residents cook for themselves. Staff will show you once, and then leave you to it.
sectionText: A catered house would be easier to run and worse for everyone in it. The habits that hold up after move-on are the ones practised here, and feeding yourself cheaply and reliably is near the top of that list.

quote.text: I could not have told you how to cook a chicken when I arrived. The first time I made dinner for four people in the house, I rang my sister about it.
quote.author: Resident

afterQuote: Shared meals are not compulsory, but most houses drift into eating together a few nights a week. It turns out to be one of the simplest ways people get to know each other.
bullets: A weekly cleaning rota agreed by the house
Labelled storage so everyone's food stays theirs
Basic equipment provided, replaced when it wears out
Nobody cleaning up after you, including staff
closing: Budgeting, shopping and cooking are unglamorous, and they are also three of the things that decide whether independent housing works out.
Residents who leave able to feed themselves for the week are in a materially stronger position than those who cannot.

title: Talking to family again, at a pace that holds
author: Admin
excerpt: Trust comes back through small kept promises, not big speeches. A visit that happens when it was supposed to happen does more than any apology.
intro: Families arrive hopeful and exhausted in roughly equal measure. They have usually heard promises before, and they are bracing for this one to go the same way.
We support contact at a pace everyone can manage, including the relative who is not sure they want contact yet.
sectionText: A phone call before a visit. A short visit before a day out. Each step kept to, before the next one is offered. It feels slow from the inside and it is the fastest route we know.

quote.text: My mum did not want to see me for the first two months. What changed her mind was not what I said, it was that I kept ringing on Sundays like I said I would.
quote.author: Former resident

afterQuote: Where there are children involved, contact runs alongside whatever formal arrangements exist. We work with those, never around them.
bullets: Guided visits in a setting that suits everyone
Family sessions with a worker present
Honest guidance on what helps and what does not
Support for relatives who are not ready yet
closing: Some relationships do not come back, and pretending otherwise does residents no favours.
Accepting that without treating it as a failure of recovery is its own piece of work, and one worth doing with support rather than alone.

title: Going back to work without knocking recovery over
author: Admin
excerpt: Full time work in week two is rarely the win it looks like. Starting smaller protects the thing that makes work possible at all.
intro: Work is good for recovery. Money, structure and a reason to be somewhere all help. The timing is what people get wrong.
A full time job in the second week often means missed meetings, missed check-ins and a resident who is too tired to notice they are struggling.
sectionText: A few shifts, a course or some volunteering gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the risk. It can always be scaled up, which is easier than scaling back after something goes wrong.

quote.text: I took forty hours a week because I wanted to prove something. I lasted a month. Second time around I started with two days and kept the job for two years.
quote.author: Former resident

afterQuote: Residents in work keep their house responsibilities. Meetings and check-ins move around shifts, but they do not quietly disappear.
bullets: CVs, applications and interview practice
How to talk about gaps and convictions
Benefits, ID documents and bank accounts
Courses and apprenticeships, where work is not the right next step
closing: A job is worth having because of the life it supports, not the other way around. When work starts eating the things that keep someone well, it has stopped being a win.
Raise it with your key worker early. Hours can usually be adjusted before anything breaks.
